$description: Type, weight, size, rhythm and motion primitives. Three families with three distinct jobs — display carries the voice, sans does the work, mono aligns the digits. Every family declares a real fallback stack, because a webfont that fails to load must degrade to something with similar metrics rather than to Times. Each webfont family also declares the weight axes it actually needs, under $extensions, so the generated fonts.css requests exactly those and no more.

display.$description:
Headings and display type only. Matthew Carter drew Verdana for on-screen reading at small sizes: exaggerated counters, wide sidebearings, and unambiguous letterforms — the same design intent as the interface face, from thirty years earlier. That shared lineage is why it is here. The previous display face was Bodoni Moda, and a didone is the precise opposite of a legibility face: its whole character is extreme hairline-to-stem contrast, which is beautiful and is the first thing to disappear for a reader with low vision. A system claiming accessibility is enforced rather than promised should not have been setting its own headings in the least legible thing on the page.

It is also a system font, present on effectively every machine, so the display face now costs zero webfont bytes. The generator noticed on its own — a family with no declared axes is not requested, so Bodoni left the generated fonts.css without anyone editing a URL.

The cost is real and worth stating: Verdana and Atkinson Hyperlegible are both humanist sans faces, so headings no longer contrast with body text by SHAPE. That contrast has to be carried by size, weight and tracking instead, which is what the display line-height and letter-spacing tokens below are now tuned for. No lower size bound any more — the didone had one because its hairlines vanished under 20px, and Verdana has no hairlines to lose.

sans.$description: Every interface surface — labels, body, buttons, help text. Commissioned by the Braille Institute and drawn specifically so that low-vision readers can tell characters apart: the letterforms are differentiated at the points where sans-serifs normally collapse into each other — I/l/1, O/0, b/d/p/q — rather than being unified for rhythm. Choosing it is not decoration. This system's whole claim is that accessibility is enforced by measurement rather than promised, and the face carrying 90 percent of its words is the largest legibility decision available. The Next revision is used rather than the 2019 original because the original ships only 400 and 700, and the interface leans on 500 and 600 for labels and emphasis; synthesising those weights would undo the drawing.

mono.$description: Token names, hex values, code, and any column of digits. The designed companion to the sans rather than an unrelated mono, so a hex value beside body text reads as the same voice at a different pitch instead of as a foreign object — and it carries the same character-differentiation work, which matters more here than anywhere else on the page: `#0d100f` is exactly the string where confusing 0 with O costs someone real time.

bold.$description: Display face only. A 700 in the UI sans reads as shouting at these sizes; hierarchy is carried by size and colour instead.

display.$description: The display size. It used to double as a floor — a didone's hairlines dropped out below it — but Verdana has none to lose, so this is a step on the scale, not a limit.
Loosened from the 1.08 a didone wanted. Verdana has a much larger x-height and longer ascenders, so 1.08 collides descenders with the line below on any heading that wraps.

Large type needs negative tracking, and Verdana needs more of it than most: its generous sidebearings are what make it legible at 11px and what make it look loose and juvenile at 40px. Tightening here is the single change that most separates the display face from the body face now that both are humanist sans.

label.$description: Uppercase micro-labels only. Caps set at default tracking read as cramped.
